chapters.title: The town in festival lights
chapters.text: On the eve of the chariot festival the streets around the temple fill with stalls, arches of light, a giant wheel and bookstalls, and the Brahmaratha stands lit in the chariot street, its cloth gopura already raised.

chapters.title: Caturdaśī night at the temple
chapters.text: The night before the full moon is Caturdaśī, the sixth night of the utsava. Each evening the deity has gone out on a different vehicle (peacock, serpent, bull, elephant, horse); for this night the temple's order of worship gives the mahā-raṅga-pūje and the siṃha-vāhanotsava, the procession on the lion, with the savāri to the eastern kaṭṭe. The utsava-mūrti goes out among the people under the red parasol and by torchlight, carried on the head of its bearer.

chapters.title: Morning of the Koḍi Habba
chapters.text: North of the temple lies the Koṭitīrtha, and its story is the heart of the sthala-purāṇa. Brahmā, grown proud of his creation, was taught by Ṣaṇmukha that all he had came by Śiva's grace, and was sent down to earth to do penance on the western bank of the Vārāhī, where five rivers meet. There he set down the kamaṇḍalu of nectar he had brought from Satyaloka and said, “Let it become a most sacred lake.” After ages of tapas, Śiva appeared before him as a pillar of light that became a crore of liṅgas, and at Brahmā's prayer blessed the lake to hold the three and a half crore tīrthas of the worlds. So the Brahmasarovara became the Koṭitīrtha, also called Brahmatīrtha and Śivagaṅgā. Today it spreads over about four and a half acres, and on the festival day rice is offered all along its borders. On the road, sugarcane is stacked high: taking sugarcane home from the Koḍi Habba is a tradition, above all for the newly married, as a blessing for children.

chapters.title: Rathārohaṇa
chapters.text: After the special mahā-pūje, at an auspicious hour of the morning, the deity ascends the chariot: “the members of the Aithal family carry the silver mūrti to the chariot.” With it go the other forms that ride the chariot: Gōḷe-dēvaru, the bamboo shoot, the trident, Tāṇḍaveśvara and the bali-mūrtis. The assembled devotees then draw the Brahmaratha along the chariot street, and people say that at this moment the bird Garuḍa appears in the sky.

chapters.title: The Brahmaratha
chapters.note: Six wheels, forty-two feet to the kalaśa
chapters.text: The chariot is a six-wheeled syandana, its wheels eight feet across. Its fixed part, from the base to the maṇṭapa, stands about eighteen feet; with the cloth gopura and the pañcaloha kalaśa it rises to about forty-two. The beams of the base end in elephants and crocodiles, and its panels carry deities, mithuna figures, warriors and rows of swans, carved by śilpis who knew iconography and the purāṇic scenes. On the festival day it is dressed with green festoons, plantain, sugarcane, mangoes and tender jackfruit. Its age is not known; the book suggests it may come from the Keḷadi kings (c. 1600), and it resembles the Brahmaratha of Kukke Subrahmaṇya.

chapters.title: Mahā-santarpaṇe and the temple
chapters.text: At midday the mahā-santarpaṇe, the great feeding, is held and prasāda is shared. In the evening the deity descends from the chariot and, with the aṣṭāvadhāna-sēve, returns to the temple; the next day come the avabhṛtha bath in the Koṭitīrtha and the lowering of the flag. In front of the temple stands the dhvajamara, the flagstaff, renewed in 2022: Koṭeśvara is called Dhvajapura in the purāṇas, the town of the banner.

Koṭitīrtha, the temple tank north of the temple, of about four and a half acres. The purāṇa says Brahmā made it from the nectar he carried from Satyaloka in his kamaṇḍalu; it was first called the Brahmasarovara.

Koṭitīrtha, with the stone maṇḍapa and bronze Nandi built in its middle when the tank was restored in 2006. The purāṇa says the three and a half crore tīrthas dwell in it, and that whatever is done here bears fruit a crore-fold.
